chunks: Al-Aṣmaʿī said: The first of the head wounds is al-ḥāriṣah, which is the one that scratches the skin, meaning it cracks it. From this it is said: “The fuller tore the garment,” meaning he split it. Then comes al-bāḍiʿah, which is the one that cuts the flesh after the skin. Then al-mutalāḥimah, which is the one that has entered into the flesh and has not reached the simḥāq. Then al-simḥāq, which is the one between it and the bone there remains a thin membrane. Every thin membrane is a simḥāq. From this it is said: in the sky are thin layers of cloud, and on the sheep are thin layers of fat.

Then al-mūḍiḥah, which is the one that reveals the whiteness of the bone. Then al-hāshimah, which is the one that crushes the bone. Then al-munaqqilah, which is the one from which the bone fragments come out. The bone fragments are a thin layer that remains upon the bone beneath the flesh. From this is the saying of al-Nābighah: “And following them from it are the thin fragments of the brows.”

Then al-maʾmūmah, which is the one that reaches the mother of the head, namely the membrane that is upon the brain. And among head wounds and injuries is al-jāʾifah, which is the one that reaches the inner cavity in the body, and in the head, the brain.

ai.seo_question: What are the classical Arabic categories of head wounds in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This report defines the technical categories of head wounds and severe injuries, moving from superficial skin damage to wounds that expose or break bone and even reach the brain or body cavity. Its significance lies in preserving precise fiqh and lexical terminology used in legal discussions of injuries and their rulings.

en.bab-ul-qaim-publications:
Al-Asmaʿi states:
The first type of head injury (shijaj) is the hariṣah, which is the one that scratches or splits the skin. From this comes the saying, "The launderer tore (haraṣa) the cloth," meaning he ripped it.
Then comes the baḍiah, which is the injury that cuts through the flesh after the skin.
Next is the mutalahimah, which penetrates into the flesh but does not reach the thin membrane covering the bone (simhaq).
Then is the simhaq, which is the wound where only a thin layer remains between it and the bone. Every thin layer is called simhaq. This term is also used to describe thin clouds in the sky (samaʾ samahiq) and thin layers of fat on a sheep.

Following that is the muḍihah, which exposes and reveals the bone.
Then comes the hashimah, which crushes the bone.
After that is the munaqqilah, which shatters the bone into pieces, causing fragments (farash Al-ʿiẓam) - thin layers that remain on the bone beneath the flesh. The poet Al-Nabighah referenced this in his verse: "And following them are the thin fragments of their brows."

Then is the maʾmumah, which reaches the protective covering of the head (umm Al-raʾs), the membrane covering the brain.
Among other types of wounds are the jaʾifah, which penetrates into the internal body cavity or, in the case of the head, reaches the brain.
